scope: 100 reference records: principal organs, General Assembly main committees, ECOSOC functional and regional commissions, specialized agency groups, funds/programmes and other entities, ten human rights treaty bodies, the Human Rights Council, two human rights review mechanisms, seven UNFCCC constituted bodies and the Santiago technical-assistance network, the Peacebuilding Commission, the Secretary-General's Peacebuilding Fund, the Committee on World Food Security, the High-level Political Forum on Sustainable Development, Voluntary National Reviews, the United Nations Resident Coordinator system and the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework. The 12 October 2026 register extension adds 17 dated primary-source records across agriculture and food, trade, LDC development, environment, peace and digital access, distinguishing a body, a programme, a treaty process, a strategy and a grant instrument through the recordKind field. Coverage does not enumerate every subsidiary body, mandate, treaty procedure, programme or funding window; bodies, funds, instruments and mechanisms are distinct categories.
affiliation: NemoWorld has no UN affiliation, mandate or endorsement. Task suggestions and SDG mappings are NemoWorld editorial proposals, not UN instructions.

institutions.eligibility: Funds are available to developing countries seeking to meet the objectives of international environmental agreements. Support reaches government agencies, civil-society organizations, private companies, research institutions and other partners, normally through GEF implementing agencies and country endorsement.
institutions.implementationEvidence: The GEF publishes cumulative financing figures (more than 27 billion US dollars in financing, primarily as grants, and 155 billion US dollars mobilised, as reported on its own page) and replenishment cycles such as GEF-9. Reported commitments and mobilised finance are not the same as disbursement, country results or an approved application.

institutions.name: Green Climate Fund (GCF)
institutions.jurisdiction: Established in 2010 by the parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and an operating entity of the Convention's financial mechanism, supporting the Paris Agreement. It works through accredited entities and national designated authorities.
institutions.mandate: Channels and catalyses climate finance to developing countries for mitigation and adaptation through country-driven projects and programmes.
institutions.eligibility: Developing countries access funding through accredited entities, including international, regional, national and direct-access entities, working with a national designated authority; readiness support is a separate access modality.
institutions.implementationEvidence: The Fund reports cumulative commitments and the number of countries covered (over 20 billion US dollars across 134 developing countries, as reported on its own page). Committed amounts are not disbursements, project outcomes or an application decision.
institutions.publicAccessRoute: greenclimate.fund publishes the governing instrument, accreditation routes, funding proposals, portfolio data and national designated authority contacts.

institutions.name: Adaptation Fund
institutions.jurisdiction: A multilateral adaptation fund serving the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement, governed by an Adaptation Fund Board with a Secretariat, a trustee and an accreditation panel. It pioneered Direct Access and Enhanced Direct Access accreditation.
institutions.mandate: Finances concrete adaptation projects and programmes that help vulnerable communities in developing countries adapt to climate change, based on country needs, views and priorities.
institutions.eligibility: Eligible developing country Parties access funding through accredited national, regional or multilateral implementing entities; Direct Access allows accredited national entities to receive funding directly.
institutions.implementationEvidence: The Fund publishes cumulative commitments, project counts and beneficiary figures (about 1.25 billion US dollars and 183 projects with about 45.8 million beneficiaries, as reported on its own page) and an independent evaluation library. institutions.name: Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs (DPPA)
institutions.jurisdiction: A United Nations Secretariat department with a global remit for preventive diplomacy, mediation and peacebuilding. It supports the Security Council, the Secretary-General's good offices and special political missions, and has published a consolidated public record of special political mission history.
institutions.mandate: Plays a central role in United Nations efforts to prevent and resolve conflict around the world through preventive diplomacy, mediation and peacebuilding support.
institutions.eligibility: An internal United Nations department, not an application or funding route. Public research access is through published statements, special political mission records and Multi-Year Appeal reporting.
institutions.implementationEvidence: Published statements, special political mission records and reports of the Secretary-General give dated public evidence. Statements and mission records do not establish conflict resolution, country consent or a country outcome.

institutions.name: UN Peacekeeping
institutions.jurisdiction: United Nations peacekeeping operations are mandated by the Security Council and managed by the Department of Peace Operations. The official page states that over two million peacekeepers from 125 countries have served since the first mission was established in 1948.
institutions.mandate: Helps countries navigate the difficult path from conflict to peace through mandated peacekeeping operations that reduce civilian deaths and violence and increase the chance of lasting peace.
institutions.eligibility: Operations are authorised by Security Council mandates; troop- and police-contributing countries provide personnel. Public research access is through mission pages, mandates and Security Council reporting.
institutions.implementationEvidence: Mandates, mission pages and reports of the Secretary-General document authorised tasks and reporting requirements. They do not establish civilian-protection outcomes or a country's security situation.

institutions.name: Women, Peace and Security agenda (Security Council resolution 1325)
institutions.jurisdiction: A United Nations Security Council agenda initiated by resolution S/RES/1325, adopted on 31 October 2000, with later resolutions. Implementation involves Member States, United Nations entities and a system-wide coordination network.
institutions.mandate: Recognises the role of women in conflict prevention and resolution, peace negotiations, peacebuilding, peacekeeping, humanitarian response and post-conflict reconstruction, and calls for their equal participation and protection from conflict-related violence.
institutions.eligibility: Addresses Member States and United Nations system entities; civil society and women's organizations participate through national action plans and reporting routes.
institutions.implementationEvidence: Reports of the Secretary-General, national action plans and inter-agency coordination documents are public. National action plans and reports record commitments and self-reporting, not independently measured outcomes.

institutions.name: Global Digital Compact
institutions.jurisdiction: An intergovernmental framework negotiated by 193 Member States and adopted in 2024 as part of the Pact for the Future. Implementation involves governments, the private sector, technical communities, researchers and civil society, with follow-up through the United Nations.
institutions.mandate: A comprehensive framework for digital cooperation and the governance of artificial intelligence that commits governments to uphold international law and human rights online and to close digital divides.
institutions.eligibility: A commitment framework rather than a funding instrument. States implement it domestically and stakeholders participate through the official participation and follow-up routes.
institutions.implementationEvidence: Published commitment and action lists, follow-up dialogue arrangements and the planned international scientific panel on artificial intelligence are public. Commitments do not establish national connectivity, affordability or delivered access.
